challenges.opponent_argument: The brief never connects its factual assertions to a governing rule of entitlement to the urn or cremains. It asserts that appellant was not legally married, that the decedent's mother paid funeral expenses, and that the cremains were buried (u15, u19, u21, u27), but cites no authority establishing that payment of the funeral invoice transferred ownership of the urn, that burial extinguished every pleaded claim, or that lack of spousal status necessarily defeated all possible legal or equitable interests. Reciting the Rule 56 standard (u72-u76) is not substantive law establishing entitlement to judgment.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without identifying and applying the governing ownership or disposition law, the brief cannot demonstrate that appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

target.excerpt: IV. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF DEFENDANT WHEN DEFENDANT MET ALL ELEMENTS IN THE STANDARD FOR REVIEW AND WAS ENTITLED TO SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the principal merits problem. Rule 56 and the cited summary-judgment cases supply only the procedural standard; they do not establish who owned the urn, who held disposition rights in the cremains, or why the asserted facts defeated every pleaded legal or equitable claim. Nonmarriage may defeat a claim based solely on surviving-spouse status, but the brief does not identify the substantive law making that fact dispositive. Likewise, payment of funeral expenses does not establish transfer of ownership without supporting law. On this presentation, the court cannot determine entitlement to judgment as a matter of law merely from the absence of an opposition.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s only asserted basis for entitlement was his claimed status as the decedent’s surviving spouse. The record before the trial court showed that Appellant was not legally married to Angelina Johnson, that he did not pay the funeral bill, and that the cremains had already been buried; Appellant identified no competent evidence establishing any separate legal or equitable right to the urn or cremains. On this record, no genuine issue of material fact remained, and Appellee was entitled to summary judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: This needs a substantive Ohio authority on who has the legal right to control or own the urn/cremains, or else the argument should be narrowed to the fact that appellant produced no competent evidence of any cognizable entitlement. If no such authority is available from the record you supplied, do not claim that the cited facts alone made appellee entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

challenges.opponent_argument: Calling the motion "unopposed" does not satisfy the summary-judgment test the brief itself quotes. That test still requires evidence showing no genuine issue of material fact, entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and only one reasonable conclusion after viewing the evidence most strongly for the nonmovant (u52-u55); all inferences likewise must favor the nonmovant (u61). Yet the brief moves directly from failure to respond to judgment (u72-u78) without analyzing whether the movant's materials actually made that required showing.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the movant did not independently satisfy each quoted requirement, the absence of a timely opposition cannot supply the missing evidentiary or legal showing.

target.excerpt: IV. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF DEFENDANT WHEN DEFENDANT MET ALL ELEMENTS IN THE STANDARD FOR REVIEW AND WAS ENTITLED TO SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited authorities support this attack. The brief correctly quotes the Ohio summary-judgment standard, under which an unopposed motion is not automatically granted; the movant must first identify admissible evidence establishing the absence of a genuine issue and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. The brief's argument section largely substitutes the word "unopposed" and a recitation of the standard for an application of the evidence to the claims. The factual narrative references exhibits, so the judgment could still be affirmed if the actual Rule 56 materials establish the necessary facts and law, but the brief itself does not demonstrate that they do.
challenges.suggested_response: Although Appellant did not file a timely substantive response, the trial court did not enter judgment by default. Appellee supported her motion with affidavits and exhibits showing the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, and Appellant identified no admissible evidence creating a factual dispute. Viewing the evidence most strongly in Appellant’s favor, reasonable minds could come to but one conclusion: Appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the Rule 56 standard, but add the specific record materials that satisfy it; do not treat the motion as granted merely because it was unopposed. If the brief cannot identify admissible evidence, say so and limit the point to appellant’s failure to create a genuine dispute after appellee made its showing.

challenges.opponent_argument: The requested relief exceeds the showing made. The brief asks the appellate court both to declare appellant a vexatious litigator and to award monetary sanctions (u100, u102), but it identifies no distinct legal basis, measure, evidentiary support, or amount for a monetary award. It also supplies no standard of review or authority permitting the appellate court to make the necessary factual findings in the first instance after the trial court denied the motion.
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if some litigation conduct were questionable, the brief has not justified reversal, an appellate designation, or any monetary sanction on the materials it identifies.

target.excerpt: For the forgoing reasons, Appellee respectfully requests this court affirm the trial court in all respects, except for a warranted reversal of its decision to deny sanctions against Appellant, including monetary, and labeling him a vexatious litigator as that term is defined in Ohio Revised Code Sec

challenges.judge_assessment: The requested sanctions relief is not supported as framed. The brief combines a statutory vexatious-litigator declaration with monetary sanctions without identifying the source, elements, amount, or evidentiary basis for the monetary award. It also gives no standard of review or authority permitting the appellate court to make disputed statutory findings and calculate sanctions in the first instance after the trial court denied relief. At most, a legally established error would ordinarily support reversal and remand for the appropriate proceedings, not an unexplained appellate monetary award.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee respectfully requests affirmance of the judgment in all respects. If this Court concludes any portion of the sanctions ruling should be revisited, the appropriate remedy would be reversal and remand for the trial court to determine, in the first instance, whether the statutory requirements for vexatious-litigator relief are met and what relief, if any, is appropriate. Appellee does not ask this Court to calculate a monetary sanction on the present record.

challenges.judge_assessment: The abandonment assertion is legally and evidentially underdeveloped. The brief cites no abandonment rule and relies on Barney's challenged affidavit. attacks_proposed.argument: A valid commission and seal do not establish the premise the brief itself identifies as essential: that the affiant actually signed and swore or affirmed the statement in the authorized person's presence. The brief defines an affidavit that way (u31), but its application establishes only the notary's licensing period, the date, and the document's format (u33, u37). It identifies no evidence showing personal appearance, administration of an oath, or acknowledgment. Thus, even under the brief's own definition, it has not shown that the papers were valid affidavits.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof of the required notarial act, the brief cannot establish that the challenged papers were competent affidavits merely because they bore a notary signature and seal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that the notary's signature "was not forged" is unsupported. The brief reasons from an alleged absence of evidence of forgery (u9), but supplies no comparison signature, testimony from the notary, notarial record, or other authentication. Proof that the notary's commission remained active until December 2013 (u37) shows only authority to notarize; it does not prove that this notary signed these affidavits or performed the January 2013 notarizations.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The central factual premise used to defeat the fraud challenge remains unproven, so the court cannot resolve authenticity merely from the notary's licensing status.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief improperly collapses distinct questions. Signature authentication, valid notarization, evidentiary admissibility, and fraud upon the court are not logically identical. Its conclusion—because notarization was valid, the document was properly submitted and no fraud occurred—does not address whether the affidavit contained false statements, whether the affiants had personal knowledge, or whether the paper satisfied summary-judgment requirements. The trial court's failure to object to format (u37) likewise does not adjudicate authenticity or truthfulness.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if the jurat were formally valid, that alone would not dispose of the fraud challenge or establish that the affidavit could substantively support summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: Calling the motion "unopposed" does not satisfy the summary-judgment test the brief itself quotes. That test still requires evidence showing no genuine issue of material fact, entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and only one reasonable conclusion after viewing the evidence most strongly for the nonmovant (u52-u55); all inferences likewise must favor the nonmovant (u61). Yet the brief moves directly from failure to respond to judgment (u72-u78) without analyzing whether the movant's materials actually made that required showing.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the movant did not independently satisfy each quoted requirement, the absence of a timely opposition cannot supply the missing evidentiary or legal showing.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief never connects its factual assertions to a governing rule of entitlement to the urn or cremains. It asserts that appellant was not legally married, that the decedent's mother paid funeral expenses, and that the cremains were buried (u15, u19, u21, u27), but cites no authority establishing that payment of the funeral invoice transferred ownership of the urn, that burial extinguished every pleaded claim, or that lack of spousal status necessarily defeated all possible legal or equitable interests. Reciting the Rule 56 standard (u72-u76) is not substantive law establishing entitlement to judgment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without identifying and applying the governing ownership or disposition law, the brief cannot demonstrate that appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This unsupported theory cannot eliminate material disputes over ownership, abandonment, or appellee's authority concerning the urn.

The retrieved case-management provisions use permissive and discretionary language concerning pretrial conferences and schedule modification, not absolute unreviewability [21, 39]. Moreover, those retrieved provisions concern a different local court and therefore do not supply the missing rule governing this common-pleas case.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief provides no governing authority for its claimed legal consequence that granting summary judgment automatically answers the separate pretrial issue or insulates docket management from appellate review.

attacks_proposed.argument: The requested relief exceeds the showing made. The brief asks the appellate court both to declare appellant a vexatious litigator and to award monetary sanctions (u100, u102), but it identifies no distinct legal basis, measure, evidentiary support, or amount for a monetary award. judge_assessments.assessment: This is the principal merits problem. Rule 56 and the cited summary-judgment cases supply only the procedural standard; they do not establish who owned the urn, who held disposition rights in the cremains, or why the asserted facts defeated every pleaded legal or equitable claim. Nonmarriage may defeat a claim based solely on surviving-spouse status, but the brief does not identify the substantive law making that fact dispositive. Likewise, payment of funeral expenses does not establish transfer of ownership without supporting law. On this presentation, the court cannot determine entitlement to judgment as a matter of law merely from the absence of an opposition.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asserts that appellant was never legally married to the decedent, that the decedent's mother paid the funeral and urn expenses, and that the cremains had been buried. It then concludes that appellant had no legal or equitable entitlement.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The pleadings, summary-judgment motion, and Ohio law governing disposition and possession of cremated remains as of 2011-2013 would determine whether nonmarriage and payment were legally dispositive.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited authorities support this attack. The brief correctly quotes the Ohio summary-judgment standard, under which an unopposed motion is not automatically granted; the movant must first identify admissible evidence establishing the absence of a genuine issue and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. The brief's argument section largely substitutes the word "unopposed" and a recitation of the standard for an application of the evidence to the claims. The factual narrative references exhibits, so the judgment could still be affirmed if the actual Rule 56 materials establish the necessary facts and law, but the brief itself does not demonstrate that they do.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It quotes Rule 56, Temple, Delker, Mers, and Williams; states that the motion was unopposed; and asserts elsewhere that exhibits established nonmarriage, payment by the decedent's mother, and burial of the cremains.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review of the complaint, the complete summary-judgment motion, its authenticated exhibits, and the trial court's entry would show whether the movant independently carried the initial Rule 56 burden.

judge_assessments.assessment: The requested sanctions relief is not supported as framed. The brief combines a statutory vexatious-litigator declaration with monetary sanctions without identifying the source, elements, amount, or evidentiary basis for the monetary award. It also gives no standard of review or authority permitting the appellate court to make disputed statutory findings and calculate sanctions in the first instance after the trial court denied relief. At most, a legally established error would ordinarily support reversal and remand for the appropriate proceedings, not an unexplained appellate monetary award.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The conclusion requests reversal of the denial of sanctions, a vexatious-litigator designation, and monetary sanctions for two years of allegedly harmful litigation. It supplies no separate monetary-sanctions analysis.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The sanctions motion, trial court's reasons for denial, any hearing record, and the specific procedural authority invoked for monetary sanctions would settle the permissible remedy and standard of review.

Because the trial court denied relief, the evidentiary and analytical omissions are particularly damaging to appellee's effort to obtain reversal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief lists proceedings, describes a barrage of filings after adverse rulings, recounts a prosecutor's warning, and declares that the conduct was harassing, maliciously injurious, unwarranted, and unsupported by good faith.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The sanctions record, pleadings and dispositions from the listed proceedings, and Ohio appellate decisions applying R.C. 2323.52 would determine whether the statutory findings were compelled or merely permissible.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abandonment assertion is legally and evidentially underdeveloped. Six years of non-removal may support an inference of abandonment, but passage of time alone does not establish every necessary element, particularly intent to relinquish the property. The brief cites no abandonment rule and relies on Barney's challenged affidavit. The attack overstates one point: ownership in Barney could still defeat appellant's claim even if it did not affirmatively establish Mitchell's ownership. Thus, this is a substantial weakness in one alternative theory, not necessarily a ground requiring reversal if other grounds independently defeat appellant's claims.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that Barney demanded removal, that appellant left the property for more than six years after eviction, and that Barney therefore legally owned anything abandoned and could dispose of it.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on abandonment of personal property, the elements of intent and relinquishment, and the complete contents and admissibility of Barney's affidavit would resolve this theory.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack exposes weaknesses in the factual presentation, but not all of its criticism is decisive. The brief says the list is nonexclusive, so enumerating six items does not by itself contradict the assertion of at least eight. Nor must every proceeding necessarily involve identical parties or claims if the conduct otherwise meets R.C. 2323.52. Still, counting the present action and its appeal as separate examples, including a police-department matter, and merely naming cases involving different defendants does not establish that appellant habitually and persistently engaged in statutory vexatious conduct. Without the underlying filings and dispositions, the list carries limited weight.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It alleges at least eight forums, introduces the six listed items with "includes but is not limited to," and describes several proceedings as concurrent, identical, or retaliatory.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete docket and pleadings from each identified matter, plus any additional matters omitted from the list, would establish the actual number, relationship, and disposition of the proceedings.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief overstates matters by saying docket management is categorically not reviewable, and Rule 56 itself does not govern whether a pretrial must occur. But the proposed attack identifies no governing common-pleas rule requiring a pretrial, and its cited local provisions concern another court and use discretionary language. If summary judgment was properly entered, there ordinarily was no trial to prepare for and no apparent prejudice from omitting a pretrial. The court would likely resolve this assignment on lack of a mandatory requirement or harmlessness rather than reverse for the brief's inadequate citation.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that summary judgment was already well-taken, a pretrial was therefore unnecessary, and the trial court could manage its docket efficiently.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The applicable Cuyahoga County Common Pleas local rules, any scheduling order promising a pretrial, and appellant's showing of prejudice would control.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract distinction among notarization, admissibility, truthfulness, and fraud is valid, but the proposed attack goes beyond the identified dispute. The assignments addressed by the brief concern the notary's commission, seal, and alleged forged signature. Nothing supplied shows that appellant preserved a separate fraud theory based on knowingly false factual content, lack of personal knowledge, or another Civ.R. 56 defect. A court would not reverse on unraised hypothetical defects. If the fraud allegation was specifically forgery, proof that the notarization was facially regular and no contrary evidence existed substantially answers it.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that the notary was commissioned, the affidavits were completed and affirmed, a seal appeared, no forgery evidence existed, and the trial court accepted the affidavits' format.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Appellant's precise assignment of error and trial-court fraud motion would show whether any substantive-falsity or personal-knowledge theory was preserved.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack would improperly require independent proof of every facially regular notarization absent some evidence contesting the notarial act. A jurat or notarial certificate ordinarily represents that the affiant appeared and swore or affirmed, and the brief expressly states that the affiants completed notarized affidavits and affirmed their truth. The attack identifies no defect visible in the certificates and no record evidence that personal appearance or administration of an oath did not occur. The brief's proof is terse, but the proposed inference that licensing and form were its only evidence misreads its express factual assertion.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It defines an affidavit as a statement sworn before an authorized person and asserts that both affiants completed notarized affidavits, affirmed their contents, and satisfied Ohio's legal requirements.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual affidavits and jurats, together with any testimony or evidence specifically disputing personal appearance or administration of an oath, would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack largely reverses the burden on the forgery allegation. Proof that a notary was commissioned does not independently prove that the notary signed a particular document, but a facial notarial certificate is not ordinarily treated as forged unless the challenger produces some evidence supporting forgery. The brief's point is that appellant produced none. Requiring comparison signatures, notarial records, or testimony merely because forgery was alleged would not follow from any authority supplied. This could matter if the document appeared irregular or appellant offered contrary evidence, but neither circumstance appears in the provided record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the signature was not forged, notes that appellant admitted the notary remained commissioned on the notarization date, and emphasizes the absence of evidence of forgery.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The challenged document, appellant's evidence of forgery, and Ohio authority on the evidentiary effect of a facially regular notarial certificate would determine whether further authentication was necessary.

results.verdict: weak on the central merits and overreaching on sanctions
results.assessment: As written, the brief is not yet persuasive on the main entitlement issue because it never connects the facts to a governing rule showing who had a legal or equitable right to the urn or cremains; the Rule 56 discussion is procedural, not substantive. The sanctions request is also too broad, because it asks for a vexatious-litigator declaration and monetary relief without a clear basis, amount, or explanation for appellate fact-finding in the first instance. The abandonment and litigation-history sections provide some support, but they are thin, partly internally messy, and do not fully carry the statutory showing. The strongest point is the overall procedural record, but the brief itself does not adequately do the legal work.

If summary judgment is affirmed, no pretrial was necessary and the issue is effectively resolved; if summary judgment is reversed, ordinary further proceedings follow without needing a separate holding that efficiency was an improper rationale. Source 44 supports the Rule 56 burden but does not support a mandatory-pretrial theory. This attack adds little beyond a1 and is unlikely to affect the disposition independently.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that the unopposed summary-judgment motion was appropriate and, once granted, made a pretrial unnecessary as a matter of courtroom efficiency.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A scheduling order or Cuyahoga County local rule expressly requiring a pretrial despite a dispositive motion could make this issue independently material.

judge_assessments.assessment: The conclusion plainly contains party-designation and pronoun errors, but the assignment of error, sanctions argument, and preceding requested relief consistently seek sanctions against Anderson and a vexatious-litigator declaration concerning him. A court would treat “against Appellee” and “her” as obvious scrivener's errors rather than construe the brief as requesting sanctions against Mitchell herself. The mistake detracts from clarity and professionalism but is unlikely to forfeit relief on an otherwise preserved issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Every substantive sanctions passage identifies Anderson as the proposed vexatious litigator and Mitchell as the party seeking relief; only the conclusion reverses those labels.

results.assessment: The brief is weakest where it needs to be strongest: it never supplies the substantive Ohio rule showing why an unmarried nonpaying person necessarily has no claim to the urn or cremains, and its summary-judgment discussion largely asserts entitlement without tying Civ.R. 56 evidence to the elements. The vexatious-litigator request is also underdeveloped because the filing list does not itself establish the required pattern or the nature of the prior proceedings. The notary-based fraud argument is the most defensible part, but it still depends on record details the brief does not squarely develop. The research leaves no settled basis for the missing substantive entitlement rule.

It identifies no intervening transfer, third-party rights, or other irreversible consequence; it identifies only the recording itself. challenges.judge_assessment: This exposes the central defect. On the supplied record, the only identified act of execution is recording a certified copy of the quiet-title judgment. The brief does not explain why reversal could not restore the parties’ legal positions, permit correction or cancellation of the recorded judgment, or otherwise affect title. Source 74 supports only the narrower proposition that recording and passage of title are distinct; it does not itself decide mootness, but it reinforces the need for the missing remedial analysis. Because mootness turns on whether effective relief remains available, the Court would need authority specific to satisfaction or execution of quiet-title judgments before accepting the brief’s categorical premise.
challenges.suggested_response: The appeal is moot because Appellants allowed the trial court's judgment to be executed and identify no relief this Court could now grant that would change the judgment already entered below. Appellants did not obtain a stay before execution, moved for one only after the judgment had been recorded, and have pointed to no authority showing that reversal could provide any practical relief on this record. At most, their filing asks for an advisory ruling on a judgment that has already been carried out.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say recording the certified judgment automatically made the appeal impossible to remedy unless you can cite authority for that proposition. Revise the mootness point to rest on the lack of any stay and the fact that Appellants identify no relief that would change the operative judgment, while avoiding an overbroad statement about recordation alone.

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited authorities, as presented, support the general mootness test but do not establish the dispositive bridge proposition that recording a certified quiet-title judgment automatically moots an appeal. Source 74 does not directly resolve that issue, yet it confirms that recordation has a limited legal function and cannot substitute for analysis of whether appellate relief remains possible. This attack substantially overlaps a2 but properly targets the authority gap rather than only the factual/remedial gap. If no controlling execution-or-satisfaction precedent supports the Eighth District’s rule, the brief’s principal basis for declining jurisdiction is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: The authorities Appellants cite do not create a right to appellate review after execution of the judgment. The proper inquiry remains whether this Court can still afford meaningful relief, and Appellants have not identified any relief that would alter the judgment already executed and recorded below. Their requested review would therefore be purely academic.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add authority, if you have it, equating execution of the judgment with mootness in this posture; if you do not, soften the claim and frame it as a practical-relief argument rather than a categorical rule.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands well as a textual attack on forfeiture. The brief itself describes the Stovalls as arguing that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution. That position appears to dispute the legal effect of recording even if it accepts that recording occurred. Corporex supports refusing to consider an issue omitted from a jurisdictional memorandum, but it does not establish omission here. The brief’s use of “concedes” blurs concession of a historical fact with concession of mootness. The Court could still find the memorandum inadequately framed, but the present materials do not justify categorical forfeiture.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not meaningfully develop a justiciability argument. Their memorandum acknowledges that the judgment was executed before they appealed or sought a stay and then asks the Court to reach the merits anyway. But merely asking the Court to overlook mootness is not the same as showing that a live controversy remains.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop saying Appellants forfeited mootness if the memorandum can fairly be read as arguing against the legal consequence of execution. Instead, say they never develop a justiciability argument and, in any event, concede execution before appeal.

challenges.opponent_argument: The assertion that the appeal presents only settled-law error correction overlooks the unresolved premise on which the appellate dismissal rested: whether recording this particular quiet-title judgment made reversal ineffectual. challenges.why_it_matters: A disputed rule governing when appellate review of quiet-title judgments disappears is a legal question capable of prospective application, not merely a request to reweigh evidence in this case.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack identifies a real weakness, but it depends on treating the recordation-and-mootness issue as a proposition actually presented by the appellants. The brief’s assertion that the case is only error correction is overstated if the jurisdictional memorandum challenges the legal rule that recording extinguishes appellate review. O’Malley and the Baughman concurrence support the Court’s institutional focus on law rather than case-specific correction, but they do not show that the specific mootness question is settled. challenges.opponent_argument: The case cannot fairly be reduced to an ordinary Rule 56 dispute. According to the brief itself, the Eighth District did not reach summary judgment and instead dismissed because the prevailing party recorded a quiet-title judgment before the notice of appeal. Whether that unilateral act extinguishes appellate review is a distinct procedural and property-law question. Record title can affect possession, while Ohio law also recognizes that title may pass without recording, underscoring that recordation and substantive ownership are not interchangeable. [74]
challenges.why_it_matters: The broader question concerns the availability of appellate review after rapid recording of a title judgment, not merely fact-bound error correction in one summary-judgment proceeding.

challenges.judge_assessment: This reframing has force because the Eighth District’s dismissal rests on a procedural mootness rule rather than on the underlying Rule 56 analysis. But source 74 does not establish that the mootness question is broad, unsettled, or of public and great general interest; it only distinguishes record ownership issues from recording. Moreover, the brief answers that the appellants did not present the mootness question as a proposition of law. The attack therefore improves the possible framing but does not itself show that this Court should accept jurisdiction.
challenges.suggested_response: This appeal is not a broad property-law case warranting this Court's review. The Eighth District dismissed it because Appellee executed the judgment before Appellants sought appellate relief, and the memorandum in support of jurisdiction does not identify any unsettled rule that would justify this Court's intervention. Appellants' complaints about summary judgment therefore remain, at most, case-specific claims of error in an already-executed judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Reframe the case as a discretionary-jurisdiction and mootness matter, not merely a summary-judgment dispute. Make clear that the merits issues are secondary and that the appeal was dismissed because execution occurred first.

challenges.opponent_argument: Admissibility and authentication do not themselves establish entitlement to summary judgment. The brief says eight exhibits were submitted and generally asserts that they were authenticated, but it does not identify which affidavit authenticated which exhibit, state the governing substantive elements for declaring the deed fraudulent and void, or explain how the cited materials conclusively established every required element. Summary judgment still requires both the absence of a genuine material dispute and legal entitlement to judgment; it is not established merely by producing authenticated documents. [77]
challenges.why_it_matters: The absence of contrary exhibits cannot cure a failure by the movant to carry the initial substantive burden. Without an element-by-element showing, the conclusion that judgment was proper does not follow.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is doctrinally correct: authentication plus the opponent’s silence does not itself establish entitlement to judgment, and the movant retains the initial burden on every substantive element. The brief does not set out the elements of the quiet-title or fraud theory or connect each item of evidence to those elements. Source 77 provides only a generic illustration of Civ.R. 56 and does not substantively establish the governing burden here. attacks_proposed.argument: The brief never establishes that recording the quiet-title judgment made effective appellate relief impossible. It identifies no intervening transfer, third-party rights, or other irreversible consequence; it identifies only the recording itself. Ohio title law distinguishes recordation from the passage of title—a deed need not be recorded to pass title—so the mere existence of a recorder filing does not, without further analysis, establish that reversal could have no practical effect. attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If recording alone is not legally equivalent to irreversible satisfaction, the Eighth District’s stated ground for dismissal fails and the appeal remains justiciable.

attacks_proposed.argument: The case cannot fairly be reduced to an ordinary Rule 56 dispute. According to the brief itself, the Eighth District did not reach summary judgment and instead dismissed because the prevailing party recorded a quiet-title judgment before the notice of appeal. Whether that unilateral act extinguishes appellate review is a distinct procedural and property-law question. Record title can affect possession, while Ohio law also recognizes that title may pass without recording, underscoring that recordation and substantive ownership are not interchangeable. [74]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The broader question concerns the availability of appellate review after rapid recording of a title judgment, not merely fact-bound error correction in one summary-judgment proceeding.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that the appeal presents only settled-law error correction overlooks the unresolved premise on which the appellate dismissal rested: whether recording this particular quiet-title judgment made reversal ineffectual. attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A disputed rule governing when appellate review of quiet-title judgments disappears is a legal question capable of prospective application, not merely a request to reweigh evidence in this case.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes the central defect. On the supplied record, the only identified act of execution is recording a certified copy of the quiet-title judgment. Source 74 supports only the narrower proposition that recording and passage of title are distinct; it does not itself decide mootness, but it reinforces the need for the missing remedial analysis. results.assessment: The brief has some force in resisting forfeiture and in recasting the case as more than an ordinary Rule 56 fight, but its main problem is fatal if not fixed: it never explains why recording the quiet-title judgment made effective appellate relief impossible. It treats recordation as if it automatically mooted the appeal without showing any irreversible consequence or authority for that leap. The forfeiture point is also overstated, because the appellants appear to have disputed the legal effect of execution, not merely the historical fact. The public-interest and constitutional-question framing is thin. The research did not supply controlling precedent settling the recordation-and-mootness issue.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack identifies an internal tension in the brief. Acknowledging that recording occurred is not necessarily conceding that recording legally mooted the appeal. The brief itself describes the Stovalls as arguing that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution, which may amount to a challenge to execution's asserted mootness effect. Corporex supports refusing to consider issues omitted from a jurisdictional memorandum, but it does not resolve whether this issue was actually omitted. The attack could defeat the forfeiture characterization, although the actual memorandum—not supplied here—would control.
challenges.suggested_response: The Stovalls do not meaningfully dispute the mootness ruling. Their memorandum acknowledges that Lender executed the judgment before they appealed and, at most, asks this Court to reach the merits anyway. That is not a developed argument that the appeal is not moot, and it supplies no basis for this Court to disturb the Eighth District’s dismissal.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Soften the forfeiture language. Replace the claim of concession with a statement that the memorandum does not develop a meaningful mootness challenge and instead asks the Court to reach the merits despite execution of the judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The mootness argument never establishes its indispensable premise: that recording a certified quiet-title judgment exhausted every effective appellate remedy. Ohio title authority recognizes that recording and ownership are not identical—an unrecorded deed may pass title, while record title may affect possession. Thus, the legal consequences of recording require analysis; labeling recording as “execution” does not itself prove that reversal could afford no relief.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof that the recording created an irreversible condition or eliminated all effective relief, the conclusion that the appeal is purely academic does not follow.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief improperly equates Lender’s unilateral recording of the judgment with the Stovalls’ voluntary satisfaction or abandonment of their claims. Ohio mootness materials distinguish voluntary relinquishment—such as a tenant voluntarily vacating—from other postjudgment events. Here, the brief alleges action by the prevailing party, not voluntary compliance or relinquishment by the appellants.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the appellants did not voluntarily satisfy or abandon the controversy, the principal rationale ordinarily supporting satisfaction-based mootness is absent.

attacks_proposed.argument: Failure to obtain a stay does not, standing alone, establish mootness. Ohio authority treats a stay and supersedeas bond as mechanisms for suspending enforcement pending appeal. That procedural mechanism does not itself answer the separate question whether an appellate court can still grant effective relief after enforcement activity occurs.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief cannot convert the timing of the stay request into a categorical bar to appellate review without separately demonstrating that no remedy remained available.

attacks_proposed.argument: The claimed “concession” is overstated. The brief itself describes the jurisdictional memorandum as arguing that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution. Accepting that execution occurred is not the same as conceding the disputed legal proposition that execution made the appeal moot, particularly where Ohio mootness treatment turns on circumstances such as voluntary relinquishment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the memorandum disputed the legal effect of execution, the Court need not treat the central mootness issue as conceded or forfeited merely because the underlying recording was acknowledged.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that a merits ruling “would not change the outcome below” is circular. The outcome below was a judgment determining title, and Ohio authority recognizes that ownership of record title can determine the right to possession. If the underlying judgment were reversed, the legal basis for treating that judgment as dispositive of title and possession would necessarily be called into question.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A live controversy remains if reversal can alter the parties’ competing claims to ownership or possession, even if the prevailing party recorded the judgment before the appeal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The filing cannot be reduced entirely to routine summary-judgment error correction while the brief simultaneously relies on a broader legal proposition—that recording a certified quiet-title judgment automatically moots a later appeal. Ohio authority indicates that recording, passage of title, record ownership, and possession are distinct concepts, making the legal effect of recording a judgment a separate question from whether the trial court weighed summary-judgment materials correctly.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the appeal presents a recurring legal question about when enforcement of a title judgment eliminates appellate relief, the “mere error correction” characterization is incomplete.

attacks_proposed.argument: Calling the matter a “run-of-the-mill” Rule 56 dispute does not address the consequence assigned to the judgment: alteration of record title and the resulting right to possession. Ohio authority recognizes that record-title questions can control possession and that recording is not invariably what passes title. The brief therefore must analyze the title-related legal issue rather than infer lack of general importance solely from the procedural vehicle used below.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The fact that judgment was entered under Rule 56 does not by itself establish that the underlying title and appellate-mootness questions lack broader significance.

attacks_proposed.argument: The number of exhibits and the presence of affidavits do not establish that every fact necessary for judgment was supported by admissible evidence. Authentication addresses whether an item is what it purports to be; it does not by itself resolve hearsay or other substantive admissibility issues. Ohio authority confirms that evidentiary rules and hearsay objections remain distinct concerns and that an affidavit is not automatically admissible for every purpose merely because it is sworn.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Because the brief does not analyze the contents, personal-knowledge foundation, or admissibility of each material item, it has not shown from the supplied materials that Lender satisfied her initial Rule 56 burden; the nonmovants’ lack of competing exhibits cannot cure that omission.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief answers the due-process claim only by identifying theoretical procedural options—discovery and opposition briefing—without addressing the Stovalls’ stated allegation that their evidence was ignored and that their opportunity was not fair. Ohio procedural authorities recognize that an opportunity to respond must be meaningful and must adequately inform a party so the evidence can be effectively rebutted; it is not necessarily enough that a nominal opportunity existed.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Absent facts establishing adequate notice, access to the pertinent evidence, and meaningful consideration of the response actually filed, the brief has not eliminated a substantial due-process question merely by showing that procedural mechanisms were available in the abstract.

attacks_proposed.argument: The merits assertion that the Stovalls “declined to meaningfully participate” is broader than the brief’s own account. That account says Marreitta filed an opposition, while only AdeWe filed none. A short or unsuccessful response is still participation, and the adequacy of the opportunity cannot be resolved solely by page count. Authorities addressing procedural fairness emphasize whether the party was adequately informed and able to rebut the opposing evidence.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The blanket nonparticipation premise cannot support rejection of both appellants’ due-process claims without separately analyzing what notice and meaningful opportunity each appellant received.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes the central merits gap in the mootness theory. Hunter and In re L.W. supply the general rule that courts do not decide academic questions, but the brief does not connect that rule to the particular act of recording a certified quiet-title judgment or explain why reversal could not restore the parties' title positions. Source 38 does not itself decide appellate mootness, but it supports the narrower point that recording, title, and possession are distinct concepts. The Eighth District's decision directly supports the result reached below, and forfeiture may prevent this Court from revisiting it, but if the mootness issue was preserved, the unexplained absence of an effective remedy is a serious vulnerability.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lender recorded the certified judgment before the appeal and stay motion, the trial court described the judgment as already executed, the Eighth District dismissed the appeal as moot, and the Stovalls omitted any challenge to mootness from their jurisdictional memorandum.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive research would be Ohio authority addressing whether recording a quiet-title judgment, without a third-party transfer or other irreversible change, constitutes satisfaction or execution that moots an appeal and whether an appellate court can order correction of the land records after reversal.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's statement that a merits ruling could not change the outcome is inadequately explained. The judgment itself declared the competing deed void and determined title. On this record, there is no identified third-party transfer or other circumstance showing that reversal could not alter record title or possession. Source 38 supports the practical relationship between title and possession, though it does not establish the appellate remedy. This attack substantially overlaps a1 but correctly identifies why the missing-remedy analysis matters.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that none of the merits issues would change the outcome below and that the appeal therefore would be purely academic, but it does not identify what part of the title determination became legally irreversible upon recording.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research should identify the statutory mechanics for recording, vacating, or correcting a quiet-title judgment and Ohio decisions addressing appellate reversal after such a judgment has been recorded.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack identifies an internal tension in the brief. Acknowledging that recording occurred is not necessarily conceding that recording legally mooted the appeal. The brief itself describes the Stovalls as arguing that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution, which may amount to a challenge to execution's asserted mootness effect. Corporex supports refusing to consider issues omitted from a jurisdictional memorandum, but it does not resolve whether this issue was actually omitted. The attack could defeat the forfeiture characterization, although the actual memorandum—not supplied here—would control.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the memorandum did not challenge mootness and conceded satisfaction, while also characterizing it as arguing that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The Court would need the exact language of the Stovalls' jurisdictional memorandum, especially page 2, to determine whether they merely acknowledged recording or disputed its legal effect on mootness.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited materials concern voluntary vacation of premises in eviction cases and do not establish that Ohio's postjudgment mootness doctrine always requires voluntary satisfaction by the appellant. The brief relies on execution by the prevailing party after no stay was in place, not on abandonment of the appeal. The attack therefore imports a voluntariness requirement that its sources do not support for this quiet-title judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lender, as the prevailing party, executed the judgment by recording it before the Stovalls appealed or sought a stay; it does not claim that the Stovalls voluntarily performed or abandoned their title claim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Controlling Ohio Supreme Court cases on involuntary execution or satisfaction of judgments would be necessary before asserting that voluntariness is indispensable.

judge_assessments.assessment: The general distinction between obtaining a stay and determining mootness is sound, but the attack does not meet the brief as written. The brief does not say that failure to seek a timely stay, standing alone, mooted the appeal; it says the judgment had already been executed by recording and that the lower courts treated that execution as dispositive. The cited stay and bond authorities do not address whether effective relief remains after recording a quiet-title judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on both the absence of a pre-execution stay and the asserted completed execution of the judgment, reinforced by the trial court and Eighth District rulings.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority addressing the consequences of enforcing a quiet-title judgment before a stay is sought, rather than general stay procedure, would be required.

judge_assessments.assessment: The asserted recurring question about the effect of recording appears to arise from appellee's mootness defense, not from the propositions the Stovalls asked this Court to accept. On the supplied record, their stated grounds challenge evidentiary sufficiency, admissibility, abuse of discretion, and due process. Source 38 does not show that they presented a broader proposition about appellate relief after recording. The brief's error-correction characterization is therefore supported unless the omitted jurisdictional memorandum framed that question expressly.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the Stovalls presented only fact-bound challenges to the trial court's summary-judgment ruling and no unsettled proposition of law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The exact propositions of law and supporting argument in the jurisdictional memorandum would determine whether a recurring mootness question was actually presented.

judge_assessments.assessment: A judgment's importance to the parties and its effect on title or possession do not make the case one of public or great general interest. Source 38 explains aspects of title and possession but identifies no conflict, recurring statewide uncertainty, or unsettled legal rule implicated by this case. The brief's analysis is terse, but the attack supplies no affirmative jurisdictional reason for review.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief characterizes the case as a routine application of Civ.R. 56 based on one movant's evidentiary submission and the opposing parties' failure to submit competing evidence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A district conflict, recurring split over quiet-title procedure, or evidence that the same legal issue affects cases statewide would be needed.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack is speculative on this record. It identifies possible distinctions among authentication, hearsay, personal knowledge, and admissibility but points to no defect in a particular affidavit or exhibit. Source 68 concerns admission of affidavit evidence at an eviction trial and does not establish that properly made affidavits are inadmissible under Civ.R. 56. Bradford and Parker support affidavit authentication of other summary-judgment materials. Although exhibit count alone proves nothing, the brief also asserts compliance with Rule 56 and notes the absence of any cognizable objection or contrary evidence.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lender submitted sworn affidavits and authenticated supporting materials satisfying Civ.R. 56, while the Stovalls offered no evidence and identified no cognizable ground of inadmissibility.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A viable attack would require the actual affidavits and exhibits and identification of a concrete defect involving personal knowledge, competency, authentication, hearsay, or failure to establish an element of the quiet-title claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited authorities concern specialized notice requirements in subsidized-housing proceedings and do not establish a deficiency in this common-pleas summary-judgment process. The record states that Marreitta filed an opposition and that both appellants had opportunities for discovery and evidentiary submissions. Nothing supplied shows defective service, inadequate notice, denial of access to evidence, or refusal to consider a properly submitted evidentiary item. A bare assertion that evidence was ignored does not create a substantial constitutional question.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief answers that the Stovalls had a fair opportunity to conduct discovery and submit briefing and evidence, and cites Maney and Goldfuss for the consequence of failing to use available procedures.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual docket, service history, scheduling orders, opposition papers, and identification of the allegedly ignored evidence would be needed to support a meaningful-opportunity claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The phrase "declined to meaningfully participate" overstates the record as to Marreitta because the brief acknowledges that she filed an opposition. But the brief does not literally claim that neither appellant participated; it argues that Marreitta's response lacked evidence and substantive law and that AdeWe filed nothing. Page count alone would not establish inadequate participation, yet this rhetorical overstatement does not show a due-process violation. The cited subsidized-housing authorities do not supply the missing record facts about notice or inability to respond.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly distinguishes Marreitta's two-page, evidence-free opposition from AdeWe's failure to respond and argues that both had an available opportunity to be heard.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The contents of Marreitta's opposition and the allegedly ignored evidence would determine whether the court failed to consider a properly presented response rather than merely rejecting an unsupported one.

results.verdict: Partly persuasive, but vulnerable on the central mootness an
results.assessment: The brief has a usable core: it ties the mootness argument to the timing of execution and argues the Stovalls have not shown a live controversy. But it is exposed where it matters most, because it never explains why recording the certified quiet-title judgment necessarily exhausted every effective appellate remedy or why reversal could not affect record title or possession. The claim that the Stovalls “do not even challenge” mootness also reads overstated if their memorandum did ask the court to reach the merits despite execution, so the forfeiture framing may be shaky. The research does not settle the actual contents of that memorandum, which would control the concession issue.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief acknowledges that this Court had held that a policy could not be amended to reflect statutory changes occurring during the two-year guarantee period (u91, u94). Westport relies principally on decisions from other districts and concedes that a conflict concerning this precise issue had been certified to the Ohio Supreme Court (u95). Its proposed distinction—that S.B. 267 predated the guarantee period—is asserted without supplying language from this Court's decision demonstrating that the holding was limited on that basis.
challenges.why_it_matters: On the authorities presented in the brief, Westport has not shown that this Court should disregard its own contrary precedent and affirm as a matter of law under S.B. 97.

target.excerpt: This Court has previously held that a policy cannot be amended to reflect statutory changes that occur during the two year guarantee period. Storer v. Sharp, Cuyahoga App. No. 86525, 2006-Ohio-1577, at P 15 (attached as Exhibit 19). Storer is distinguishable from the situation in the present case wh

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack on Westport's S.B. 97 ground. The brief acknowledges binding Eighth District language in Storer against incorporating a statutory change during the two-year guarantee period, and it further acknowledges that Advent and Storer produced a certified conflict on essentially the question presented here. Decisions from other districts do not permit this Court simply to disregard its own precedent. Westport offers a factual distinction based on S.B. 267 having preceded the guarantee period, but the brief does not demonstrate from Storer that this distinction removes the case from its holding. Unless later controlling authority resolved the conflict in Westport's favor, the S.B. 97 theory is materially vulnerable. Westport would lose this alternative basis for affirmance, though its out-of-state-policy ground could still sustain judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: To the extent Storer is read to bar incorporation of statutory changes during a guaranteed period, Westport submits that Storer is distinguishable on these facts. The Westport coverage was first written when S.B. 267 was already in effect, and the January 1, 2002 renewal occurred after S.B. 97 became effective. Under Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, the law in effect at renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage; thus, as of the January 1, 2002 renewal, Ohio law did not require Westport to offer UM/UIM coverage, and such coverage could not be implied as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not make S.B. 97 the sole pillar of affirmance unless you have controlling Ohio Supreme Court authority resolving the Advent/Storer conflict. Keep this point as an alternative and frame it narrowly: the Westport coverage was first written after S.B. 267 took effect and was renewed after S.B. 97 became effective.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack identifies a genuine limitation in the brief's presentation: the schedule is expressly a schedule of covered autos the insured owns, and the brief does not reproduce the liability-coverage symbols or provisions for hired and nonowned autos. Thus, the schedule alone does not necessarily establish the entire vehicle scope of the policy. But an Ohio workplace and the theoretical possibility of hired or nonowned Ohio vehicles are not evidence that any Ohio-registered or principally Ohio-garaged vehicle was covered. Plaintiffs would need record evidence, or policy language making the omission legally material, rather than speculation. The attack could defeat the vehicle-premise portion of summary judgment if the policy symbols show broader coverage, but it does not independently overcome proof that the policies were issued for delivery outside Ohio.

Because R.C. 3937.18 applies only to policies issued for delivery in Ohio with respect to Ohio vehicles, the statute does not apply on this record.

The brief supplies neither the complete insuring agreement nor authority resolving that language.

challenges.judge_assessment: As to the excess policy considered on its own terms, this attack lands. The brief's statement that the policy can pay above a retained limit where primary insurance is not afforded is facially broader than a purely follow-form excess grant. The later assertion that automobile coverage is subject to the underlying policy's terms may ultimately foreclose UM/UIM coverage, but the brief does not quote enough of the insuring agreement, retained-limit provision, definitions, or exclusions to establish that result. Nor does it cite authority making absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage categorically dispositive. Westport risks losing summary judgment on the excess-policy theory unless the complete policy demonstrates that the retained-limit coverage does not encompass the claim. Because the underlying auto policy is not subject to R.C. 3937.18 on this record, the excess policy likewise does not give rise to implied UM/UIM coverage. The retained-limit language does not convert the excess policy into a separate Ohio automobile liability policy.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal observation is correct but does not fairly describe Westport's reasoning. The brief does not use the absence of an Ohio UM/UIM endorsement as the sole or necessary proof of statutory inapplicability. It principally relies on asserted Pennsylvania delivery and the Florida and Pennsylvania garaging of the scheduled autos. The endorsement's absence is at most corroborative. Removing that fact leaves the principal argument intact, so little turns on this attack.

judge_assessments.assessment: This reads the cited authorities too narrowly. The brief quotes decisions stating that the law in effect at an actual renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and Arn is presented as applying S.B. 97 to a post-effective-date renewal without requiring a separate endorsement expressly reciting the statute. Issuance of a renewal policy without Ohio UM/UIM coverage may itself constitute the relevant incorporation. The stronger objection is the contrary Storer precedent, not the absence of a document expressly saying S.B. 97 is incorporated.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on former R.C. 3937.18(E), Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for the proposition that statutory changes could be incorporated at renewal and that the law effective at renewal governs.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full opinions in Arn, Advent, and St. Clair would confirm whether they required an express policy amendment or treated renewal under the new law as sufficient.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief does not say the originating agreement is wholly unavailable; it says no physical policy was printed for the one-month period and that the binder evidencing that coverage was produced. It also cites an affidavit and interrogatory answers for inception and renewal dates. Plaintiffs' missing-policy theory therefore does not itself create coverage or a factual dispute. A concrete conflict in the binder's terms could matter, but the proposed attack identifies none and substantially overlaps the more focused renewal attack in a6.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Westport says the binder, both annual policy sets, interrogatory answers, and an affidavit were produced, and that plaintiffs cited no law making nonproduction of a nonexistent printed policy a basis for implying coverage.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief adequately distinguishes express policy coverage from coverage sought by operation of law. It states that the $50,000 UM/UIM grant applies to owned autos only, while Press was driving his own vehicle and not a vehicle described as covered under any Westport policy. That is a failure to satisfy the coverage grant, not necessarily reliance on an exclusion. Without policy language or evidence suggesting that Press's personal vehicle qualified as an owned auto of the named insured, the existence of limited express UM/UIM coverage does not preserve his claim.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that UM/UIM coverage is limited to owned autos, that the scheduled autos were located in Florida and Pennsylvania, and that Press was driving his own undescribed vehicle at the time of the accident.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The UM/UIM endorsement's insured and covered-auto definitions would conclusively confirm the point.

The mere fact that those exhibits are not reproduced in the supplied text does not establish a record deficiency. A valid challenge would have to show that the cited exhibits were absent from the appellate record, inadmissible, or insufficient—not simply unavailable in this excerpt.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable main theme: it presses an out-of-Ohio delivery theory and a renewal-based S.B. 97 theory, and the record fragments it cites do support that broad direction. But it is vulnerable in three places. First, the Storer point is its sharpest weakness because the brief does not show why binding Eighth District language does not control. Second, the delivery showing is thin if the record really contains only addresses and counsel’s assertion, rather than concrete delivery proof. Third, the Commercial Excess Policy discussion is underdeveloped because the retained-limit language may be broader than the brief acknowledges. The vehicle-coverage premise also feels incomplete as presented.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a substantial attack on Westport's alternative S.B. 97 ground. The brief expressly acknowledges adverse Eighth District precedent in Storer and a certified interdistrict conflict that remained pending when the brief was filed. An Ohio appellate panel ordinarily follows its own district's precedent unless Storer is materially distinguishable or has been displaced by intervening Supreme Court authority. Westport offers a distinction—S.B. 267 predated the start of this guarantee period—but the passages supplied do not establish that Storer's holding was limited to periods beginning before S.B. 267. Shay is described only negatively; saying it did not forbid all mid-period changes does not affirmatively establish that S.B. 97 governed this renewal. The attack could defeat the alternative statutory-amendment rationale, though not the independent out-of-state-policy rationale.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport need not ask this Court to decide the broader conflict between Storer, Advent, and the cases cited by appellants. Even if the Court were to set the renewal issue aside, summary judgment is still proper because the Westport policies were not issued for delivery in Ohio with respect to motor vehicles registered or principally garaged in Ohio, and R.C. 3937.18 therefore does not apply.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not make the S.B. 97 point do independent work unless you can distinguish Storer with a record citation or controlling authority. The safer course is to treat the renewal-date discussion as unnecessary to affirmance and to rest the answer on nonapplicability of R.C. 3937.18 to the policies.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport treats the Pennsylvania address of the named insured and the Kansas address of the insurer as conclusive proof that the policies were not delivered or issued for delivery in Ohio (u40). But the brief identifies no mailing record, delivery testimony, application, broker evidence, or policy provision establishing where delivery occurred. That omission is significant because Westport's own formulation of R.C. 3937.18 and its cited cases treat delivery or issuance for delivery as a distinct statutory requirement (u34, u41, u45, u51).
challenges.why_it_matters: If the place of delivery is unsupported rather than established, Westport has not conclusively proved a necessary premise of its principal statutory argument and summary judgment cannot rest on that premise.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a focused problem with extending the principal R.C. 3937.18 argument to the Commercial Excess Policy. The brief acknowledges that the excess policy identifies no vehicles and has retained-limit coverage, yet treats it as covering only the autos scheduled in the underlying Business Auto Policy. The cited auto-policy cases support nonapplication of R.C. 3937.18 to policies delivered outside Ohio for out-of-state vehicles, but the brief does not show that they resolve the statutory characterization of this particular umbrella form. Westport does offer contract language—that the excess policy is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary insurance—but the retained-limit provision creates a facial reason to inspect the complete excess form rather than assume complete identity. The attack threatens judgment on the excess policy, not necessarily the Business Auto Policy.
challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy does not supply an independent UM/UIM grant. To the extent any automobile coverage exists in the excess form, it is follow-form coverage tied to the underlying Business Auto Policy, and appellants have identified no language in the excess policy that separately creates UM/UIM coverage beyond that underlying coverage.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the excess-policy argument so it does not assume the umbrella form is automatically identical to the auto policy in every respect. If the brief cannot quote the excess form, it should say only that appellants have not identified any independent UM/UIM grant in that policy.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport's categorical assertion that the Commercial Excess Policy supplies coverage only when the underlying policies do is inconsistent with its own description of the excess contract. The brief states that the policy pays both amounts above primary insurance and amounts above a retained limit for certain injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded (u24). That retained-limit feature indicates at least some coverage can exist without corresponding primary coverage. Westport therefore cannot establish the asserted linkage merely by calling the policy excess or by noting the absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage.
challenges.why_it_matters: Unless the actual excess-policy language specifically excludes UM/UIM claims or confines all automobile coverage to coverage afforded by the primary policy, the absence of primary UM/UIM coverage does not by itself entitle Westport to judgment on the excess policy.

challenges.opponent_argument: The quoted text of R.C. 3937.18(E) says only that nothing prohibits an insurer from incorporating permitted statutory changes at the beginning of a policy period (u63-u64). Westport repeatedly converts that permission into automatic incorporation, asserting that Senate Bill 97 simply "became incorporated" on January 1, 2002 (u89-u90). The brief does not identify language in the renewal policy, a notice, endorsement, or other act showing that Westport actually exercised the statutory permission. Its own cited formulations say changes "could be" or "can" be incorporated, not that every intervening amendment automatically becomes part of every renewal (u65, u78-u81, u85).
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof of actual incorporation, the statutory amendment's effective date alone does not establish that the renewal eliminated previously existing UM/UIM rights, leaving Westport short of its summary-judgment burden.

challenges.judge_assessment: The linguistic point is fair but likely not decisive as framed. R.C. 3937.18(E), as quoted, permits incorporation; it does not itself say every statutory amendment is automatically incorporated. Westport sometimes says the changes 'became incorporated' without identifying a separate endorsement or notice. But the brief also argues that the law in effect at an actual renewal governs the scope of statutorily required UM/UIM coverage, relying on Arn, Advent, and St. Clair. If those cases hold that the governing statute changes at renewal without a policy endorsement, no additional proof of an affirmative incorporation act is needed. Source 1 is unrelated landlord-tenant authority and does not support this attack. Thus the attack exposes imprecise reasoning but depends on the full cited insurance decisions and policy-renewal record.
challenges.suggested_response: Because the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, after S.B. 97 took effect, the relevant statute is the version in force at the time of renewal. Westport does not contend that a separate endorsement was required to make the statute applicable at renewal; the point is that the renewal was governed by the law then in effect.
